meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There Are Two Lasting Bequests We Can Give Our Children: Roots and Wings'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Beecher. Quote Investigator traces it to Hodding Carter's 1953 Where Main Street Meets the River, where he credits an unnamed "wise woman."

answer.label: Not Henry Ward Beecher — an anonymous saying popularized by Hodding Carter
answer.authorName: An unnamed “wise woman,” quoted by Hodding Carter
answer.authorDates: Recorded in 1953 · Hodding Carter II, 1907–1972, Pulitzer-winning Mississippi newspaper editor
answer.sourceLine: The earliest strong match Quote Investigator could locate ↗ is in Hodding Carter’s 1953 book Where Main Street Meets the River (Rinehart & Company), page 337 — and Carter did not claim the line. He wrote that “a wise woman once said to me” it, and never named her. Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence that Henry Ward Beecher, who died in 1887, ever used the expression; the Beecher credit is traceable to a 1982 Ronald Reagan message, twenty-nine years after the saying’s first documented printing and ninety-five after Beecher’s death.

source.excerpt: A wise woman once said to me that there are only two lasting bequests we can hope to give our children. One of these she said is roots, the other, wings. And they can only be grown, these roots and these wings, in the home.
trail: 1953 — the earliest strong match. Quote Investigator locates it in Hodding Carter’s Where Main Street Meets the River, page 337 ↗, where Carter reports it as something “a wise woman once said to me.” The book’s 1953 Rinehart publication is confirmed by its Open Library catalog record ↗.

May 1953 — mass circulation. Quote Investigator records a Reader’s Digest reprint that same year ↗, tidied into the quotation-mark form and credited to Carter’s book. Newspaper instances follow through the later 1950s, increasingly without any attribution at all.

9 September 1982 — the Beecher credit appears. Ronald Reagan’s Grandparents Day message ↗ states “Henry Ward Beecher once wrote” and gives the saying. Quote Investigator documents no earlier Beecher attribution.
The Beecher record is silent. Wikiquote’s Beecher page ↗ contains no roots-and-wings line, and Quote Investigator reports no substantive evidence that he used the expression ↗.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗, which records the citation as verified on paper.

source.rightsNote: The wording everyone quotes first appears in Where Main Street Meets the River, published by Rinehart & Company in 1953 ↗ — well after the 1931 cutoff for the United States public domain — so the passage is treated here as in copyright. Because Carter attributed the sentence to a woman he never identified, no earlier, public-domain printing of it has been found.

author.name: Hodding Carter II
author.kicker: The editor who wrote it down
author.heading: Who Hodding Carter actually was
author.bio: William Hodding Carter II was an American journalist who founded the Delta Star in Greenville, Mississippi and merged it into the Delta Democrat-Times, which he edited until failing eyesight led him to hand it to his son, Hodding Carter III, in 1966. He won the 1946 Pulitzer Prize for Editorial Writing for pieces attacking racial intolerance, including the editorial “Go for Broke” defending Japanese American servicemen. Where Main Street Meets the River (1953) is his memoir of that newspaper career — and the book that put “roots and wings” into general circulation, though Carter carefully credited the words to someone else.

misattribution.heading: Where the credit went wrong
misattribution.intro: This is an orphan saying that has been assigned at least three famous parents, none of whom can be shown to have originated it. Hodding Carter printed it first — and disclaimed it in the same sentence.

items.why: Quote Investigator states it found no substantive evidence that Beecher used the expression ↗. The credit surfaces in Ronald Reagan’s Grandparents Day message of 9 September 1982 ↗ — “Henry Ward Beecher once wrote” — and again in John Connally’s 1993 memoir. Beecher died in 1887, sixty-six years before the saying’s earliest documented printing, and Wikiquote’s Beecher page ↗ has no trace of it.

items.who: Jonas Salk (via Chicken Soup for the Soul, 1993)
items.why: Bettie B. Youngs’ essay in the 1993 collection reports Salk telling her that good parents “give their children roots and wings.” Quote Investigator notes this appears many years after Carter’s 1953 instance was already circulating ↗, and suspects Salk was relaying a saying he had heard.

Carter’s printed sentence reads “there are only two lasting bequests we can hope to give our children. One of these she said is roots, the other, wings.” The hedges came off fast: Quote Investigator records that the May 1953 Reader’s Digest reprint deleted “she said” and added quotation marks ↗, and by 1959 it was running as an anonymous adage.

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody knows who said it first. What is documented is that the earliest strong match is Hodding Carter’s 1953 Where Main Street Meets the River, page 337 ↗ — and Carter attributed it to a woman he never named.

context.heading: Why this one stuck to Beecher
lead: The saying travelled the way most orphan aphorisms do: through condensation. Carter’s 1953 sentence is hedged and conversational — “a wise woman once said to me,” “only two,” “hope to give.” Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ shows the hedges being sanded off almost immediately: Reader’s Digest reprinted it in May 1953 with the “she said” deleted and quotation marks added, and by 1959 an Altoona newspaper was running it as an unattributed adage with no wise woman at all.

Once a line is floating free of its author, it needs one, and a famous nineteenth-century preacher is a cheap fit for anything that sounds like a sermon. The credit to Beecher becomes visible in the record on 9 September 1982, in Ronald Reagan’s Grandparents Day message ↗ — and a presidential document is exactly the kind of citation that a quotation dictionary will copy without checking.
context.detailsSummary: The other names in the file
detailsBody: Jonas Salk. The polio researcher is often given the “roots to know where home is, wings to fly away” variant. It reaches print in Bettie B. Youngs’ essay in the 1993 collection Chicken Soup for the Soul, where she reports Salk saying it to her. That is four decades after Carter’s book; Quote Investigator suspects Salk, if he said it, was repeating something already in circulation ↗.

A 1920 near-miss. Quote Investigator notes a 1920 Smith Alumnae Quarterly book review headed “Roots and Wings” that uses both metaphors for a young woman’s development — but it explicitly says the passage “does not really fit” the saying under investigation and treats it only as a thematic precursor, not an earlier version.
Jean Wade Rindlaub. A 1963 religious magazine quoted the advertising executive expanding the saying at an American Mothers’ Committee meeting — another repeater, not an originator.
context.pull: Carter went out of his way not to take credit. Everyone since has been happy to hand it to someone else.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest strong match is Hodding Carter, Where Main Street Meets the River (Rinehart & Company, 1953), chap. 27, p. 337, where Carter credits an unnamed "wise woman"; QI found no substantive evidence Beecher used the expression; QI records the May 1953 Reader's Digest reprint, the 1959 unattributed Altoona Mirror instance, the 1963 Jean Wade Rindlaub instance, Reagan's 9 Sept 1982 Beecher attribution, the 1993 Chicken Soup / Jonas Salk instance via Bettie B. Youngs, the 1993 John Connally Beecher attribution, and the 1920 Smith Alumnae Quarterly item described as a thematic precursor that 'does not really fit'.

Ronald Reagan's Message on the Observance of Grandparents Day, dated 9 September 1982, states: "Henry Ward Beecher once wrote, 'There are only two lasting bequests we can hope to give our children. One of these is roots . . . the other, wings.'"

Wikiquote's Henry Ward Beecher page contains no roots-and-wings or 'two lasting bequests' line in any section, and gives his dates as 24 June 1813 – 8 March 1887, describing him as an American Congregationalist clergyman, social reformer and speaker.

Hodding Carter (William Hodding Carter II) was born 3 February 1907 and died 4 April 1972; he was a journalist and newspaper editor associated with the Greenville Delta Democrat-Times, won the 1946 Pulitzer Prize for Editorial Writing for editorials on intolerance including 'Go for Broke', and Where Main Street Meets the River (New York: Rinehart & Co., 1953) is listed among his works.
Open Library holds a catalog record for the work 'Where Main Street meets the river' by Carter, Hodding, first published 1953, publisher Rinehart.

WIST Quotations records the quotation as from Hodding Carter II, Where Main Street Meets the River, 'It's How We Like It' (1953), and notes it is almost always quoted without Carter's note about the 'wise woman'.
Henry Ward Beecher's Wikipedia article describes him as an American Congregationalist clergyman, social reformer and speaker (used only as the identity link for the misattributed name).
